analysis.one_liner: Orders Treasury to identify and break up banks and insurers too big to fail.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee in April 2012, and no committee vote or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Secretary, within 90 days of becoming law, to list every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company whose failure would damage the economy badly enough to require a taxpayer bailout [S2]. Starting a year later, Treasury would then break up each of those institutions so no single company's collapse could again force a bailout [S2]. It never advanced beyond being referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who bore the cost of the 2008 bailouts and would face less risk of paying again for the failure of a single giant financial company. Small and mid-sized banks also stand to gain by competing against less sprawling rivals.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Treasury to publish a list of any bank, investment bank, hedge fund, or insurance company whose failure would hit the U.S. or global economy catastrophically without government assistance [S2].
Directs Treasury to break up every institution on that list so that its failure would no longer require a taxpayer bailout [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The largest U.S. financial firms — big banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurers — whose sprawling size and implicit government backstop would be dismantled.

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'too big to fail' only as an entity so large its failure would have a 'catastrophic effect' on the financial system or economy, giving the Treasury Secretary wide discretion over which firms get broken up and how [S3].

It gives Treasury one year to carry out breakups with no stated process or criteria for dividing the firms, an approach an honest supporter would acknowledge is blunt compared with the case-by-case resolution authority regulators already had under the 2010 Dodd-Frank law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — making sure no single company's failure can force another taxpayer bailout — addresses a real cost ordinary people paid in 2008. But the bill is mechanically crude: it hands the Treasury Secretary a list-and-dismantle assignment with vague criteria and a one-year deadline, instead of using the more gradual resolution process created by the Dodd-Frank law two years earlier. Supporters who care about the outcome could fairly be told the tool was blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the two-year Congress ended with no vote anywhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman (D-CA), for himself and Rep. Maurice Hinchey, introduced the bill on April 26, 2012, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services that same day.
The action history ends there: the bill never received a committee markup, a committee vote, or a House floor vote during the remainder of the 112th Congress.
Only one member, Rep. Hinchey (D-NY), cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest U.S. banks, insurers, and hedge funds are better off: the bill that would have directed Treasury to break up firms 'too big to fail' never advanced, so none of the largest financial companies faced forced restructuring during the 112th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest banks and their shareholders

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; after its April 2012 referral, the committee took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee, where it sat, took no action.

industries.industry: Largest U.S. banks and financial conglomerates
industries.note: The bill would have required Treasury to break up any bank whose failure would demand a taxpayer bailout, ending the implicit government backstop that makes giant banks cheaper to fund and more profitable [S2]. The industry benefits from that backstop at the public's expense, so its interest in stopping the bill ran against ordinary taxpayers.

industries.industry: Systemically important insurers and hedge funds
industries.note: The bill's breakup mandate covered insurance companies and hedge funds deemed too big to fail, not just banks [S2]. Firms in this group that rely on an implicit federal safety net lose it.

Dismantling sprawling mega-banks would reduce the competitive advantage their size and government backstop give them, opening space for smaller banks. The bill record does not show these banks lobbying for it; this follows from the bill's effect on market structure.
